name: Liberalism in the United States
summary: The American liberal tradition rests on the founding's Lockean principles: equal natural rights, government by consent, constitutional limits, free speech and religion, and separation of church and state. From the Progressive Era and especially Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal, it added an active federal government that regulates business, supports organized labor, taxes progressively and provides social insurance, on the view that freedom also needs economic security. At its mid-century peak it joined this mixed economy with civil rights, Keynesian economic management, free trade and an anticommunist internationalism built around the UN and the Western alliance.
scope: The mainstream American liberal tradition of the New Deal and its heirs, as the defining sources describe it (the Miller Center essay on Truman's domestic affairs, the Alterman and Mattson history of American liberalism, the Stanford Magazine essay on modern American liberalism and Cold War liberalism): Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal and Second Bill of Rights, Truman's Fair Deal, Kennedy's liberalism and Johnson's Great Society. Answers rest on those presidents' own speeches and on the Declaration of Independence. It excludes libertarianism, American conservatism, the New Left and the contemporary Democratic program (modern-liberalism-in-the-united-states), whose later positions on abortion, LGBT rights, climate and gender this profile leaves null.
